walkthroughs.body_html:
Physical Chemistry — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Physical Chemistry brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Physical Chemistry.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: For a process to be spontaneous, what must happen to the total entropy of the universe?
options: Enantiomers are the same molecule drawn differently on paper.
The entropy of the system must increase for the process to be spontaneous.
The entropy of the surroundings must stay constant for the process to be spontaneous.
It must increase (ΔS_total > 0) — the system's entropy alone can decrease as long as the surroundings' entropy increases more.

mcqs.q: What is the relationship between two enantiomers?
options: They are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions but have identical chemical and physical properties otherwise.
Enantiomers are the same molecule drawn differently on paper.
Enantiomers have different boiling points and react completely differently with all reagents.
A buffer destroys added acid by changing it into water vapour.

mcqs.q: How does a buffer maintain its pH when small amounts of acid are added?
options: A buffer destroys added acid by changing it into water vapour.
The entropy of the surroundings must stay constant for the process to be spontaneous.
A buffer prevents any H+ ions from being added to the solution at all.
The conjugate base in the buffer reacts with added H+ to remove it, keeping pH nearly constant.
